messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 125 m (approximate; within 5% means roughly 119 to 131 m). Motor class at most G, an upper limit rather than a requirement, since the flyer has no certification (fixed). No rail length, wind or landing limit is stated, so I assume the 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind and the usual 6 m/s touchdown limit. One stage is enough at this altitude.
2. Feasibility: 125 m is a low flight. Ignoring drag it needs v = sqrt(2*9.81*125) = 49.5 m/s at burnout, and a light rocket loses a large share of its ideal height to drag, so the real figure is higher. An A or B motor in a small airframe is the natural size; a C would already overshoot a light build, and using the G ceiling would mean a deliberately heavy rocket, which makes no sense for an uncertified flyer. I need real impulse and thrust data for the small-motor candidates before sizing.

2. Feasibility: the C6 returns 8.8 N*s over 1.83 s with a loaded mass of 23.1 g, while the A8 (2.2 N*s) and B6 (4.3 N*s) both come back listing only a 0 s ejection delay, so neither can time a chute deployment near apogee. The C6 in a deliberately stout airframe is the practical pick and it sits far under the G ceiling. As an upper bound, 8.8 N*s on about 0.08 kg gives 8.8 / 0.08 = 110 m/s of ideal delta-v, well above the 49.5 m/s ballistic figure even after heavy drag losses.
3. Size: I am aiming at roughly 0.08 kg loaded: a 41.6 mm tube 0.45 m long, a 0.11 m hollow plastic ogive nose, an 18 mm motor mount and three balsa fins. Thrust-to-weight = 4.8 / (0.08 * 9.81) = 6.1, above the 3:1 minimum. With average thrust alone, a = (4.8 - 0.08 * 9.81) / 0.08 = 50.2 m/s^2 and rail exit would be sqrt(2 * 50.2 * 1.5) = 12.3 m/s, under the 15 m/s gate; but the C6's 14.1 N ignition spike dominates the short rail stroke, so the real exit speed should be well above the constant-thrust figure. Descent mass is about 0.08 - 0.011 = 0.069 kg. For a 5 m/s sink rate under Cd 0.8 the canopy needs A = 2 * 0.069 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.055 m^2, a diameter of sqrt(4 * 0.055 / 3.1416) = 0.26 m, so a 0.35 m canopy leaves margin. Burnout is at 1.83 s and apogee should come near 4 s, so the 3 s delay ejects close to the top.
4. Draft: 0.56 m long, 41.6 mm diameter, about 0.08 kg loaded, C6-3 motor, 0.35 m chute, 3 fins at the tail for margin on the short fat tube. Checking it in the simulator.

4. Check: the simulator gives an apogee of 177.0 m against the about-125 m goal, 42% high and well outside the 5% band, so this draft fails the altitude target. Every gate passed: rail exit 16.6 m/s (at least 15), thrust-to-weight 5.1 (at least 3), margin 1.99 cal at rail exit (at least 1.0), landing 4.6 m/s (under 6), chute out at 4.9 s. Liftoff mass came back 0.0957 kg, already heavier than my 0.08 kg estimate, and it still overshot, so mass alone is not the lever.
5. Fix: apogee 177.0 m needs to come down about 30%. Added weight cannot do that on a rocket this draggy, so I am adding frontal area instead: the body goes from 41.6 mm to 50 mm diameter, keeping the same tube length, wall and layout so loaded mass stays near 0.10 kg. Rough drag scaling puts the new apogee around 120 to 130 m. The wider reference shrinks the margin in calibers: 1.99 * 0.0416 = 0.083 m of physical margin, which on a 50 mm reference is still 0.083 / 0.05 = 1.7 cal, above the gate. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: apogee 133.9 m is closer but still 7% over the 125 m goal, above the top of the band at about 131 m. Two gates now fail as well: rail exit 13.7 m/s is under 15, and the rail-exit margin of 0.99 cal is a hair under the 1.0 minimum. Landing 5.2 m/s, deploy at 4.9 s and thrust-to-weight 4.0 all pass. The wider tube came back heavier than I estimated, at 0.121 kg loaded, which explains both the slow rail exit and the lost margin.
5. Fix: apogee 133.9 m is about 9 m high, rail exit 13.7 m/s is under 15, and margin 0.99 cal is under 1.0. I need less mass and a bit more drag at the same time: the tube grows to 54 mm diameter but shortens to 0.40 m with a thinner 0.8 mm wall, the nose swaps the hollow polystyrene shell for a lighter solid balsa ogive, and the chute drops to 0.30 m, which still lands under 6 at this weight. Fins grow to 0.11 m root and 0.065 m span to hold margin on the shorter, fatter airframe. Expected mass near 0.095 kg, which should put rail exit back over 15 m/s and apogee close to 125 m.

4. Check: apogee 133.8 m is still about 7% over the 125 m goal and out of the band. Worse, the shorter rocket dropped the rail-exit margin to 0.49 cal, under the 1.0 minimum, and rail exit is still 14.0 m/s, under 15. Landing 5.8 m/s, deploy at 4.9 s and thrust-to-weight 4.2 all pass. Mass only fell to 0.117 kg, so the lightening bought almost nothing while the shorter body pulled the CP forward.
5. Fix: the C6's 8.8 N*s is simply too much impulse for this airframe. Apogee 133.8 m is over the band, rail exit 14.0 m/s and margin 0.49 cal both fail, and on a C6 every cure for one makes another worse. I am stepping down a motor class to a B-class motor with a real ejection delay, which cuts impulse roughly in half and drops about 14 g of motor mass. Looking up candidates.

5. Fix: the B7 returns 5.0 N*s, 7.2 N average thrust and only 9.1 g loaded at 13 mm diameter — half the C6's impulse and 14 g lighter, with delays out to 10 s. The C4 is no help (8.9 N*s is the same impulse as the C6), so the B7 it is. New sizing on the B7: keep the 41.6 mm tube for drag but back to 0.35 m of it, a 0.10 m solid balsa ogive, a 13 mm mount, and three balsa fins at the tail. Estimated liftoff mass about 0.055 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 7.2 / (0.055 * 9.81) = 13.3. Rail exit on average thrust alone: a = (7.2 - 0.055 * 9.81) / 0.055 = 121 m/s^2, so v = sqrt(2 * 121 * 1.5) = 19 m/s, comfortably over the gate. Descent at about 0.05 kg under a 0.25 m canopy: v = sqrt(2 * 0.05 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 0.049)) = 4.5 m/s. Apogee is the open question: half the impulse on roughly half the mass lands somewhere around 120 to 140 m. Burnout is at 0.69 s and apogee should come near 4.5 s, so the 4 s delay ejects at about 4.7 s, just past the top.

4. Check: the simulator gives an apogee of 134.6 m — better, but still 7.7% over the 125 m goal and above the top of the band near 131 m. Everything else now passes: rail exit 25.1 m/s (at least 15), thrust-to-weight 12.2 (at least 3), margin 1.52 cal at rail exit and through the burn (at least 1.0), landing 5.3 m/s (under 6), and deployment at 4.7 s right at apogee at only 0.4 m/s. Liftoff mass came back 0.06 kg, close to my 0.055 kg estimate.
5. Fix: apogee 134.6 m still misses the band by about 8 m, and that was the third fix round, so I stop here. About 10 g of added mass or a slightly fatter tube would probably close the gap, but I will not make a fourth change blind.
6. Uncertainty: the design is safe but about 8 m high on apogee. Drag on a small rocket is a model value, so a real build could land inside the band or further out; roughly 10 g of nose weight would shave a few metres and raise the margin. The 5.3 m/s descent also sits close to the 6 m/s limit if the chute comes out small.
messages.content:
Apogee B7-4 on a 41.6 mm airframe, 0.45 m long, 0.06 kg loaded.
Simulated: 134.6 m apogee — still about 8 m over the 125 m goal after three fix rounds; all safety gates pass (25.1 m/s rail exit, 1.52 cal margin, 5.3 m/s landing).
